vocab: She never watches TV in the morning.
We often meet at the park.
After school, I go to the library.
In my free time, I draw.
He practises the guitar every day.

grammar.title: Present simple + how often?
grammar.rule: I / you / we / they play  -  he / she / it plays. The frequency word goes before the verb: I usually play. But after be: I am often late.
examples: How often do you read?
She never plays video games.
We sometimes go swimming.

4E-01.pronunciation: The -s of he / she / it: plays and reads sound like [z], walks and likes sound like [s], watches and practises add a syllable [iz].
4E-01.did_you_know: In the UK, the school day usually ends around half past three. Many secondary schools offer after-school clubs: sport, drama, music, coding...
4E-01.model:
Alex: I usually play football after school. I sometimes read in the evening.
Sam: I often read after school. I never play football on weekdays.
Alex: What do you like doing?
Sam: I like drawing because it helps me relax.

listening.title: Free time
questions: What sport does Tyrone want to try?
How old is he?
On which two weekdays is the training?
listening.fallback:
Receptionist: Good afternoon, Riverside Swimming Pool.
Tyrone: Hello! I'd like to join the water polo club, please.
Receptionist: Of course. How old are you?
Tyrone: I'm fifteen.
Receptionist: Then you're in the junior team. Training is on Tuesdays and Thursdays, from half past six to eight.
Tyrone: Great, thanks a lot!

go_further.title: Stop wasting time
go_further.task: Tom can't concentrate on his homework. Note three things that distract him.

practice: Circle the correct sentence: I usually read / I read usually.
Complete: She ___ (play) tennis on Mondays.
Ask your partner: How often do you read? Write the answer.
Write two sentences about a hobby you like and one reason.
4E-01.mission: Interview a partner about three after-school activities. Report two similarities or differences.
can_do: I can say how often I do an activity.
I can ask: How often do you...?
I can explain why I like an activity with because.
4E-01.memory: Without looking, write five frequency or hobby words; check, correct, and reuse two in sentences.

4E-02.hook: ONE SATURDAY. TWO FRIENDS. ONE PLAN!
vocab: What do you do in your free time?
We could go bowling on Saturday.
The bowling alley is near the station.
How about going to the park?
Let's stay in because it's raining.

grammar.title: Making suggestions
grammar.rule: Let's + verb  -  We could + verb  -  How about / What about + verb-ing? Answer: Good idea! / I'd rather + verb...
examples: Let's go to the cinema.
We could visit the museum.
How about going bowling?

4E-02.pronunciation: Go up at the end of a yes/no question: Do you want to come? Go down for a suggestion: Let's go to the park.
4E-02.did_you_know: British teenagers often say "Fancy going to the cinema?" to make a suggestion. Fancy + verb-ing = Ça te dit de... ?
4E-02.model:
Mia: What shall we do on Saturday?
Leo: We could visit the park.
Mia: I'd rather go to the cinema because it's raining.
Leo: How about visiting the museum?
Mia: That sounds great! Let's meet at two.

listening.title: Making plans
questions: What are the friends planning?
Which activity do they finally choose?
When do they plan to meet?
listening.fallback:
Gemma: It's Jack's birthday this weekend. Let's organise a surprise!
Makayla: Good idea! How about the cinema?
Gemma: Hmm, we saw that film last week. And ice skating? No, Jack doesn't like it.
Makayla: Everybody likes bowling. Let's go bowling!
Gemma: Perfect. Let's meet on Saturday at three, in front of the bowling alley.

go_further.title: Going to the cinema
go_further.task: Tamara and Mario choose a film. Note the time of the film and the time they meet.

practice: Complete: We could ___ (visit) the park.
Complete: How about ___ (go) to the cinema?
Write a polite refusal and an alternative suggestion.
With a partner, agree on two activities and one meeting time.
practice_answers: Réponse possible: I'd rather visit the museum. How about Saturday?
4E-02.mission: In pairs, plan a Saturday with a budget and weather constraint. Make suggestions, justify a preference and agree on a plan.
can_do: I can make a suggestion with let's, we could or how about.
I can refuse politely and suggest something else.
I can agree on a time and a place.
4E-02.memory: Recall five expressions for suggesting, agreeing or preferring. Use three in a short dialogue.

vocab: Our project is a reading club.
Our aim is to help new students.
The main benefit is less waste.
We want to improve the playground.
We will organise a book sale.
First, we will ask the head teacher.
Finally, we will present our results.
It's useful because students need help.

grammar.title: Talking about plans: will / could
grammar.rule: will + verb = a decision or a plan (We will plant herbs). could + verb = a possibility (We could sell vegetables). Our aim is + to + verb.
examples: First, we will make a poster.
We could ask the science teacher.
Our aim is to reduce waste.

3E-01.pronunciation: Stress the important word in a pitch: Our AIM is to make our school GREENER. Pause after First, Then and Finally.
3E-01.did_you_know: Many schools in the UK and in France have an eco-committee: students who lead projects like recycling, saving energy or growing a garden. The international programme is called Eco-Schools (Éco-École in France).
3E-01.model: Our project is a school garden. Our aim is to grow vegetables and make our school greener. First, we will ask the science teacher for help. Then, we will plant tomatoes and herbs in the schoolyard. We could also share what we grow with other classes. We want to do this because it will help students learn about nature and work together. Finally, we will show our garden to other classes. Thank you.

listening.title: Turning plastic waste into art
questions: In which country do the Greenfingers Changemakers live?
What plastic waste do they collect? Name two things.
What do they make with it? Name two things.
What is their message?
answers: Wall murals, jewellery (earrings, bracelets, necklaces), plastic dresses, a Christmas tree
Stop using single-use plastics, or recycle them
listening.fallback: Hi, I'm Nicole. I'm a Greenfingers Changemaker in Nigeria. With my friends, we collect plastic in our streets: cups, bottles and lots of bottle caps. Then we turn this waste into art. We make wall murals with bottle-cap flowers, we make earrings and bracelets, and we even made a Christmas tree with green bottles! Our message is simple: stop using single-use plastics. And if you use them, recycle them!

practice: Underline the aim in the model.
Find two actions and one benefit.
Complete: Our aim is ___ (make) our school greener.
Write one sentence using because to justify your project.
practice_answers: Our aim is to grow vegetables and make our school greener.
Ask the science teacher; plant tomatoes and herbs; benefit: learn about nature and work together.
starters: First, we will... Then, we will...
3E-01.mission: Pitch your school improvement project to a group. Explain the aim, two actions, a benefit and answer one question.
can_do: I can present the aim of a project.
I can explain the steps with first, then and finally.
I can justify my project with because and answer a question.
3E-01.memory: Close the page: recall aim, action, benefit, first and because; use them in a mini-pitch.

vocab: I want to defend my idea.
It's a good idea. However, it's expensive.
In my opinion, we need more clubs.

grammar.title: Answering an objection
grammar.rule: Accept, then contrast: I see what you mean, but... / That's true. However, ... / Although + idea, + your answer.
examples: I see what you mean, but it only takes one hour.
That's true. However, students can choose.
Although it costs money, it's useful.

3E-02.pronunciation: Use a polite, calm voice: slow down on HOWEVER and BUT, then stress your key argument.
3E-02.did_you_know: Debating clubs are popular in British schools, and some students take part in national competitions. Good debaters listen to the other side, accept a fair point, and then explain their own argument calmly.
3E-02.model: Our school should start a reading club. It could help students discover new books. Some people might say that students are too busy. However, we could meet only once a month. This solution is practical because it does not take much time. What do you think?

listening.title: Different opinions
questions: What do Gemma and Jack disagree about?
Why does Gemma like her French teacher?
Which expression does Jack use to end the disagreement?
Which teacher do they both like?
answers: She is strict, but students learn a lot
listening.fallback:
Gemma: I really like Madame Martin, our French teacher. She's strict, but we learn a lot.
Jack: I see what you mean, but her lessons are hard for me. I don't understand everything!
Gemma: OK... let's agree to disagree.
Jack: But Miss McCloud, the science teacher, is brilliant.
Gemma: Yes, I agree with you there. She's really kind.

practice: Underline the main proposal.
Circle the objection and box the response.
Complete: We should ___ (create) a club.
Write one objection and a respectful reply using however.
practice_answers: Our school should start a reading club.
Objection: students are too busy; reply: meet only once a month.
starters: In my opinion, our school should...
I see what you mean, but...
3E-02.mission: Defend a school project with two reasons and respond politely to one objection from another group.
can_do: I can give my opinion and two reasons.
I can answer an objection politely with however or but.
I can disagree without being rude.
3E-02.memory: Without looking, recall five argument words; make a sentence with however and one with because.

vocab: It leaves at half past ten.
It arrives at a quarter to four.

grammar.title: Telling the time and timetables
grammar.rule: at + time: at 10:15 (ten fifteen / a quarter past ten). Timetables use the present simple: The train leaves at 12:30. It arrives at 18:30. Question: What time does it leave?
examples: What time does the train leave?
It leaves at a quarter past ten.
The next train arrives at platform 1.

4E-03.pronunciation: fifTEEN or FIFty? Stress the end of -teen numbers (thirTEEN, fifTEEN) and the beginning of -ty numbers (THIRty, FIFty).
4E-03.did_you_know: British timetables often use the 24-hour clock (18:30), but people usually say "half past six".
4E-03.model:
Nora: Excuse me, which platform for the Cambridge train?
Ben: The 10:15? It leaves from platform 3.
Nora: Great! What time does it arrive?
Ben: At five past eleven. I love train trips, they're relaxing.
Nora: Me too, but I hate getting up early!

listening.title: Trains and travel
questions: Which platform does the Cambridge train leave from?
In conversation C, where is the train going?
What time does Harry's ticket say?
answers: To Liverpool (her ticket is for Oxford)
listening.fallback:
Passenger: Excuse me, does the Cambridge train leave from here?
Staff: The 10:15? No, it leaves from platform 3.
Inspector: Your ticket is for Oxford, but this train is going to Liverpool.
Angel: Hurry up, Harry! The London train leaves at 4:30.
Harry: No, my ticket says 4:20! Oh look, it's late. We can catch it!

go_further.title: Travelling abroad
go_further.task: Listen to five airport announcements. Note one flight number, one gate and one time.

practice: Write the times in words: 10:15 - 12:30 - 15:45.
Complete: The train ___ (leave) at 12:30 from platform 2.
Write the question: ___ time ___ the train arrive?
Give your opinion about train trips with one adjective and because.
practice_answers: a quarter past ten - half past twelve - a quarter to four
What time does the train arrive?
Réponse possible : I like train trips because they are relaxing.
4E-03.mission: In pairs, one student reads a class-trip timetable aloud, the other notes times, platforms and one opinion. Then swap roles and check your notes together.
can_do: I can understand times and platforms in a short dialogue.
I can ask what time a train leaves.
I can note an opinion I hear.
4E-03.memory: Write five times in words and three station words. Test a partner next time.

4E-04.hook: ONE TEEN. TWO CULTURES. ONE STORY.
vocab: I visit my grandparents in July.
My half-brother lives in New York.
My best friend is from Poland.
Tacos on Sunday are a family tradition.

grammar.title: Finding key information: wh- questions
grammar.rule: Who? = a person. Where? = a place. When? = a time. What? = a thing or an activity. How often? = frequency. Underline the answer in the text before you write it.
examples: Where does Lucía live? In Manchester.
Who is her best friend? A girl from Poland.
When does she go to Mexico? Every summer.

4E-04.pronunciation: Final -s: lives and comes = /z/, visits = /s/, misses = /iz/. Say it clearly: she misses her grandparents.
4E-04.did_you_know: In the 2021 census, about one person in six living in England and Wales was born in another country.
4E-04.model: Hi, I'm Lucía. I'm 14 and I live in Manchester, but my family comes from Mexico. At home we speak Spanish and we eat tacos on Sundays. At school I speak English all day. My best friend is from Poland. Every summer I visit my grandparents in Mexico City. I miss them a lot, but I love my life in two cultures!

listening.title: Talking about your family
questions: Where does Rob, Sam's half-brother, live?
How many times has Sam visited Rob?
How old is Rob?
listening.fallback:
Jack: Hey, is that the new Game of Kings? Where did you get it?
Sam: My half-brother Rob sent it. He lives in New York.
Jack: Your half-brother? I didn't know!
Sam: Yes, he's 23, five years older than me. I've visited him three times and we often talk online.
Jack: Cool! Let's play it.

go_further.title: My town
go_further.task: Read Alex's text about his seaside town. Find his favourite beach and one activity you would like to try.

practice: Find: Where does Lucía's family come from?
Find: What language does she speak at home?
True or false? Lucía visits Mexico every winter. Correct it.
Find one thing she misses and one thing she loves.
practice_answers: False: she visits Mexico every summer.
She misses her grandparents; she loves her life in two cultures.
starters: She lives in... but her family comes from...
4E-04.mission: Read a short testimony, fill in an ID card (name, age, places, languages, traditions, feelings) and present the person to your group in three sentences.
can_do: I can find who, where and when in a short text.
I can understand feelings like miss and love.
I can sum up a testimony in three sentences.
4E-04.memory: Write five question words with one example answer each.

4E-05.hook: FIRST, THEN, FINALLY: WRITE YOUR WEEK!
vocab: First, I get up at seven.
After that, I go to school.
I like Mondays but I hate Tuesdays.
I love Fridays because we have art.
I do my homework in the kitchen.

grammar.title: Linking words to organise a paragraph
grammar.rule: Order: first, then, after that, finally. Add: and, also. Contrast: but. Reason: because. Start with a topic sentence and end with a conclusion.
examples: My week is busy but fun.
First, I go to school by bus. Then I do my homework.
I like my week, but I want more free time!

4E-05.pronunciation: Read your paragraph aloud: make a short pause after each linking word (First, ... Then, ...). Your reader follows your plan.
4E-05.did_you_know: Many British students write their homework in a planner, a small school diary that teachers and parents check.
4E-05.model: My week is busy but fun. First, on Mondays I get up at seven and I go to school by bus. Then, after school, I usually do my homework in the kitchen. After that, on Wednesdays I play basketball with my friends because I love team sports. Finally, at the weekend I relax: I read comics and I sometimes visit my cousins. I like my week, but I would like more free time!

listening.title: Using colours to do homework
questions: What colour is PE, and why?
What colour are the sticky notes for geography?
What does the pink circle on her calendar mean?
answers: Yellow, because her trainers are yellow
listening.fallback:
Student: I organise my homework with colours. First, I buy cheap pens, sticky notes and folders.
Student: Then I give each subject a colour: maths is green like my ruler, and PE is yellow like my trainers.
Student: History is blue and geography is black.
Student: Finally, on my wall calendar, a green star means a maths test and a pink circle means French homework.

go_further.title: Taking notes
go_further.task: Listen to Mark and Clare. Note two tips to make your notes shorter.

practice: Put in order: Then / First / Finally / After that.
Join with because: I like Fridays. We have art.
Join with but: I love sport. I hate swimming.
Write a topic sentence about your week.
practice_answers: I like Fridays because we have art.
I love sport but I hate swimming.
Réponse possible : My week is busy but fun.
starters: Finally... I like my week because...
4E-05.mission: Write a 70-90 word paragraph about your week with at least four linking words. Swap with a partner, colour the linking words and suggest one improvement.
can_do: I can write a topic sentence.
I can organise my ideas with first, then, after that, finally.
I can give a reason with because.
4E-05.memory: Write four order words and one contrast word. Use them in a mini-paragraph next time.

4E-06.hook: LOST IN TOWN? ASK, LISTEN, GO!
vocab: Go straight on for two minutes.
Take the first right into King's Road.
The café is next to the cinema.
The bank is opposite the school.
It's between the bank and the park.
It's on the corner of the street.
How do I get to the station?

grammar.title: The imperative for directions
grammar.rule: Use the verb without a subject: Go, Turn, Take, Walk. Negative: Don't turn left. Places: next to, opposite, between, on the corner of.
examples: Go straight on and turn right.
Don't cross the bridge.
The station is opposite the museum.

4E-06.pronunciation: Stress the key words: turn LEFT at the TRAFFIC lights. And say it politely: exCUSE me...
4E-06.did_you_know: In the UK, cars drive on the left. In London, some crossings have LOOK RIGHT painted on the road to help visitors.
4E-06.model:
Tourist: Excuse me, how do I get to the station?
Amy: Go straight on and turn left at the traffic lights.
Tourist: Left at the traffic lights. And then?
Amy: Take the second right. The station is opposite the museum.
Tourist: Thank you very much!
Amy: You're welcome.

listening.title: Giving directions
questions: Speaker A: which turn do you take, and into which street?
Speaker C: what is opposite the building?
Speaker D: which right turn do you take?
answers: The first left, into Green Street
The second right, into King's Road
listening.fallback:
Speaker A: Go straight on and take the first left into Green Street. Walk past the library: it's next to the library, on the left.
Speaker C: Go straight on past the traffic lights to the roundabout and turn left. It's next to the theatre, opposite the hospital.
Speaker D: Go straight on and take the second right into King's Road. It's next to the bookshop, opposite the café.

go_further.title: My city
go_further.task: Read the magazine page about Liverpool. Choose two places you would like to visit and say how to get there.

practice: Complete: ___ straight on and ___ left.
Translate: en face de / à côté de.
Put in order: the / first / right / take.
Give directions from your school to a shop in two sentences.
practice_answers: Réponse possible : Go straight on and turn right. The shop is next to the bakery.
starters: Excuse me, how do I get to...?
4E-06.mission: With a simple town map, play Secret Destination: give directions to a secret place, your partner follows with a finger and names the place. Swap three times.
can_do: I can ask for directions politely.
I can give simple directions with the imperative.
I can say where a place is (next to, opposite).
4E-06.memory: Draw five arrows and write the matching direction under each one.

4E-07.hook: BIG CITY OR SMALL TOWN: WHICH LIFE FOR YOU?
vocab: I take the Tube to school.
The south is warmer than the north.

grammar.title: Comparatives
grammar.rule: Short adjectives: big - bigger than, busy - busier than. Long adjectives: more expensive than. Irregular: good - better, bad - worse. Same level: as quiet as.
examples: London is bigger than Newquay.
A flat in London is more expensive.
The weather in the south is better than in the north.

4E-07.pronunciation: than is short and weak: bigger than London sounds like "bigger thn London".
4E-07.did_you_know: Cornwall, in the south-west of England, is famous for its beaches. Newquay is one of the UK's favourite surfing towns.
4E-07.model:
Zoe, London: I live in a flat in London. My school is big and noisy and I take the Tube every day. London is busier and more exciting than a small town, but it is more expensive.
Kai, Newquay: I live in a small seaside town in Cornwall. My school is smaller than Zoe's. I walk to school and I surf at the weekend. Life here is quieter and slower, but there are fewer shops.

listening.title: Weather forecast
questions: Which region may have a thunderstorm, and when?
Which region has the best weather, and how warm is it?
Is the east warmer or colder than the north?
listening.fallback:
Reporter: Here is today's weather. In the north, it's very windy and cold, about 10 degrees, so take an umbrella.
Reporter: In the east, it's rainy all day, with a storm in the afternoon, but it's a bit warmer: 13 degrees.
Reporter: The west and the middle are dry but cloudy, 10 degrees.
Reporter: The south has the best weather: sunny in the afternoon and 15 degrees.

go_further.title: My town
go_further.task: Read Alex's text about Newquay. Compare his town with yours in two sentences.

practice: Complete: London is ___ (busy) than Newquay.
Complete: A flat in London is ___ (expensive) than a house in Cornwall.
Find two differences between Zoe's and Kai's lives.
Write one sentence comparing your town with London.
practice_answers: Zoe takes the Tube, Kai walks; Zoe's school is bigger.
4E-07.mission: In groups, compare two lifestyles (city and seaside, or France and the UK) in a Venn diagram. Present three differences and one similarity.
can_do: I can find differences in two short texts.
I can compare with -er than and more ... than.
I can say which life I prefer and why.
4E-07.memory: Write five adjectives and their comparatives. Include one irregular one.

4E-08.hook: IT RAINED, WE LAUGHED, WE RAN: TELL YOUR TRIP!
vocab: I went to London last summer.
We visited the Tower of London.
I took a photo of the bridge.
We had fun on the bus.
Last summer we went to Spain.
I went to Italy two years ago.
In the end, we ran into a café.

grammar.title: Past simple
grammar.rule: Regular verbs: verb + -ed (visited, played). Irregular: go - went, see - saw, have - had, take - took. Negative: didn't + verb. Question: Did you + verb? Time: yesterday, last summer, two years ago.
examples: We visited the Tower of London.
We didn't have umbrellas.
Did you enjoy the trip?

4E-08.pronunciation: -ed endings: /t/ walked, /d/ played, /id/ visited. Only verbs ending in t or d add a syllable: vi-si-ted, wan-ted.
4E-08.did_you_know: London's red double-decker buses are famous. Some tour buses have an open top so tourists can see the sights.
4E-08.model: Last summer I went to London with my family. On the first day, we took an open-top bus tour. We saw Big Ben and the London Eye. Then it rained a lot and we didn't have umbrellas! We ran into a café and had hot chocolate. It was a funny day and I loved it.

listening.title: Tour of London
questions: How long is the bus tour?
What does a tourist ask for when it starts raining?
What happens at the end of the tour?
answers: A storm starts and everybody runs off the bus
listening.fallback:
Greg: Welcome to our two-hour tour of London on an open-top bus!
Tourist: Oh no, it's raining! Have you got any umbrellas?
Greg: Sorry, no umbrellas today. On your left, Big Ben and the Houses of Parliament.
Tourist: Is tea with the Queen included?
Greg: No, but there's a café near Buckingham Palace. Oh no, a storm! Everybody off the bus, quick!

go_further.title: Travelling abroad
go_further.task: Listen to the airport announcements. Which flight was late, and why?

practice: Write the past: go - see - have - take.
Complete: We ___ (visit) the Tower of London.
Make it negative: We had umbrellas.
Ask a question: you / enjoy / the trip?
4E-08.mission: Tell a partner about a real or imaginary trip in 6-8 sentences: where, when, what you did, a problem and how you felt. Your partner asks two Did you...? questions.
can_do: I can tell a short story in the past.
I can use regular and irregular past verbs.
I can ask a question with Did you...?
4E-08.memory: Write ten irregular verbs in the past. Make a memory game with a partner.

4E-09.hook: YOUR FRIEND DOESN'T UNDERSTAND? EXPLAIN IT SIMPLY!
vocab: I'd like a salad as a starter.
Do you mean the first dish?

grammar.title: Paraphrase: say it another way
grammar.rule: Explain a word you can't translate: It's a kind of... / It's like... / You use it to... / It means... Use short sentences and words your friend knows. Check: Do you understand?
examples: A starter is the first dish of the meal.
It's a kind of spicy chicken.
In other words, the library is closed.

4E-09.pronunciation: Speak slowly and stress the important word: it's a KIND of SOUP.
4E-09.did_you_know: In British restaurants, a "starter" is the first dish, and many people say "pudding" for any dessert.
4E-09.model:
Tom: What does "starter" mean?
Nina: It's the first dish of the meal, before the main course.
Tom: And Thai chicken?
Nina: It's a kind of spicy chicken from Thailand, with rice.
Tom: OK, I understand now. Thanks!

listening.title: Eating out
questions: What starter does Sally order?
What main course do they both choose?
What does Jamie drink?
listening.fallback:
Waiter: Good evening. A table for two?
Jamie: Yes, please. I'd like the French onion soup to start.
Sally: A tomato salad for me. And for the main course, the Thai chicken and rice.
Jamie: Steak or chicken? I can't decide... OK, the Thai chicken for me too.
Sally: And a mineral water, please.
Jamie: A fresh orange juice for me.

practice: Explain "main course" in one simple sentence.
Complete: A menu is something you read ___ choose your food.
Explain "mineral water" to a friend.
Write a question to check that your friend understands.
practice_answers: Réponse possible : It's the big dish of the meal.
Réponse possible : It's water from a spring, in a bottle.
Do you understand? / Is it clear?
4E-09.mission: In groups of three, A reads a short English menu or notice, B doesn't understand, C helps by explaining in simple English. Rotate roles three times.
can_do: I can explain a word in simple English.
I can help a friend understand a menu or a notice.
I can check that my friend understands.
4E-09.memory: Choose three new words and write a simple explanation for each one.

vocab: Put the word stress on the right syllable.

grammar.title: Word stress and intonation
grammar.rule: Each word has one strong syllable: BRIL-liant, BOR-ing, ex-CI-ting, an-NOY-ing. Yes/no questions go up at the end: Was it good? Wh- questions go down: What did you see? Show strong feelings by stressing the adjective.
examples: It was BRILLIANT!
Was it good? (up)
What did you see? (down)

4E-10.pronunciation: Small words are weak and fast: a, of, to, and. Big words are strong: a FILM of ACTION. Strong syllables make the rhythm of English.
4E-10.did_you_know: English is a stress-timed language: strong syllables come at regular intervals and small words become very short.
4E-10.model:
Ella: Did you like the film?
Sam: Yes, it was BRILLIANT!
Ella: Really? I thought it was BORING.
Sam: What did you prefer?
Ella: The cartoon. It was so FUNNY!

listening.title: Giving your opinion
questions: Which film did Jack see with his sister?
What did Gemma think of Tornado Express?
Which actor can't Gemma stand?
answers: It was brilliant: exciting, with great special effects
listening.fallback:
Gemma: Hi Jack! Have you just seen a film?
Jack: Yes, Friends Forever, with my sister Molly. I thought it was boring, but she liked it.
Gemma: I saw Tornado Express. It was brilliant, so exciting!
Jack: I want to see Double Revenge.
Gemma: Oh no, I can't stand Jessica Foster. She's so annoying!

practice: Underline the stressed syllable: exciting - annoying - brilliant - interesting.
Up or down? "Was it good?"
Up or down? "What did you see?"
Write a sentence with a strong feeling and stress the adjective.
practice_answers: Réponse possible : It was so BORING!
4E-10.mission: In pairs, perform a 6-line film review dialogue. Your partner checks the stress of three adjectives and the intonation of two questions.
can_do: I can stress the right syllable in common words.
I can make my voice go up or down in questions.
I can show my feelings with my voice.
4E-10.memory: Write five adjectives with the stressed syllable in capitals. Say them to a partner next time.

3E-03.hook: IT'S MY FAVOURITE, AND HERE IS WHY!
vocab: In my opinion, it's a great film.
For example, the ending is surprising.
Films such as Skyfall are exciting.
The main reason is the music.

grammar.title: Opinion + reason + example
grammar.rule: Point: In my opinion / I think... Reason: because / since / that's why. Example: for example, for instance, such as. A strong opinion always has a reason and an example.
examples: In my opinion, Skyfall is the best Bond film.
It has a better story than most action films.
For example, Bond seems older and more human.

3E-03.pronunciation: Pause just before because and for example: it gives you time to think and helps your listeners follow.
3E-03.did_you_know: Skyfall's theme song, sung by Adele, won the Oscar for Best Original Song in 2013.
3E-03.model: My favourite book is Wonder. In my opinion, it's the best story about school life because it shows how kindness can change everything. For example, Jack becomes Auggie's friend even when other students are cruel. Moreover, the characters are very real. That's why I recommend it to everyone in my class.

listening.title: My favourite film
questions: Who sang the Oscar-winning song from Skyfall?
Which book did speaker C read after seeing the film?
Which version of Let the Right One In does speaker E prefer?
answers: Pride and Prejudice, by Jane Austen
listening.fallback:
Speaker B: My favourite film is Skyfall. The story is better than in most Bond films, it was filmed in Shanghai and Scotland, and Adele's song won an Oscar.
Speaker C: I love Pride and Prejudice. It's about people who judge others too quickly. After the film, I read Jane Austen's novel.
Speaker E: My choice is Let the Right One In. There are two versions, and I prefer the Swedish one to the American one.

practice: Complete: I love this series ___ the characters are funny.
Add an example: The film has great special effects, ___ the flying scene.
Correct the order: For example I think that it is good.
Write a Point-Reason-Example chain about your favourite song.
practice_answers: I think it is good. For example, the ending is surprising.
3E-03.mission: Present your favourite film, book or game in one minute: one opinion, two reasons, one precise example. The group votes for the best-justified choice.
can_do: I can give my opinion clearly.
I can support it with two reasons.
I can give a precise example.
3E-03.memory: Write three ways to give a reason and three ways to give an example.

3E-04.hook: ONE IDEA. FIVE STEPS. A BETTER SCHOOL!
vocab: We propose to open a club.
The aim is to help students.
Let's set up a homework club.
Firstly, it will open on Tuesdays.
To sum up, it's a great idea.

grammar.title: Structure and check a proposal
grammar.rule: Title - Aim (We propose... / The aim is to...) - Steps (Firstly, Secondly, In addition) - Benefit (It will help... because...) - Conclusion (To sum up...). Then check: capital letters, -s, will + verb, linking words.
examples: We propose to set up a homework club.
Firstly, it will open on Tuesdays.
To sum up, it will help students organise their time.

3E-04.pronunciation: proPOSE, proPOsal: the stress is on the second syllable. Read your proposal aloud before you hand it in.
3E-04.did_you_know: The Pomodoro Technique is named after a tomato-shaped kitchen timer: "pomodoro" means tomato in Italian.
3E-04.model: A quiet homework club - our proposal. The aim of this proposal is to help students who cannot work well at home. Firstly, we propose to open a quiet room on Tuesdays and Thursdays from 4 to 5 pm. Secondly, older students could help younger ones. In addition, we would use the Pomodoro method: 25 minutes of work, then a short break. However, we need a teacher in the room. To sum up, this club will help everyone feel more organised.

listening.title: Organising your time
questions: Who invented the Pomodoro Technique, and when?
How long is one work session?
What does Peter do with his phone?
answers: Francesco Cirillo, an Italian, in the 1980s
He switches it off and uses a separate timer
listening.fallback:
Host: Peter, you get top grades. What's your secret?
Peter: The Pomodoro Technique. An Italian, Francesco Cirillo, invented it in the 1980s. The name comes from a tomato-shaped kitchen timer.
Peter: First, I list the steps of my task. Then I work for 25 minutes and take a short break of three to five minutes.
Peter: After four or five short breaks, I take a longer one. And I switch off my phone!

practice: Put in order: To sum up / Firstly / The aim is / Secondly.
Correct the mistakes: the club will helps student to work.
Add a benefit with because: The club will be useful...
Write a title and an aim for your own proposal.
practice_answers: The aim is / Firstly / Secondly / To sum up
The club will help students to work.
Réponse possible : ... because students will have a quiet place.
3E-04.mission: Write a 120-150 word proposal for a school project. Swap drafts, use the checklist (aim, steps, benefit, conclusion) and make three corrections before your final version.
can_do: I can organise a proposal in clear parts.
I can use firstly, in addition, however and to sum up.
I can proofread and correct my text.
3E-04.memory: Write the five parts of a proposal and one linking word for each.

3E-05.hook: LISTEN SMART: CATCH THE KEY IDEAS!
vocab: My teacher gave me good advice.
She advises us to sleep more.

grammar.title: Spotting arguments and intentions
grammar.rule: Advice: You should... / Don't... / Try to... Reasons: because, so, that's why. Intentions: to inform, to advise, to warn, to persuade. Notes: key words only and symbols (+ and, -> so, x don't, = means).
examples: Eat fruit + x cola
Break 5 min / 30 min
Intention -> to advise students before exams

3E-05.pronunciation: Speakers stress the important information. Write the stressed words first: TAKE a BREAK every HALF HOUR.
3E-05.did_you_know: In England, students take their GCSE exams at about 16, at the end of Year 11.
3E-05.model: Mr Hall: Good morning. Today I want to persuade you to sleep more. Firstly, teenagers need about nine hours of sleep. Secondly, sleep helps your memory, so you remember your lessons better. Finally, screens at night keep you awake, so switch off your phone one hour before bed.

listening.title: Advice for exams
questions: How long should a break be, and how often?
Which food is especially good for studying?
Where can students find past exam papers?
listening.fallback:
Teacher: Your exams are next week, so here is my advice. Don't eat sweets or drink cola: eat fruit, especially apples.
Teacher: Study in a room with plenty of light, but not too comfortable, or you'll fall asleep.
Teacher: Don't try to learn everything: learn the main points first, then the details.
Teacher: Use the past exam papers in the library, and take a five-minute break every half hour. Good luck!

go_further.title: Taking notes
go_further.task: Listen to Mark helping Clare. Note how pictures can make notes shorter.

practice: Take notes with symbols: Eat fruit and avoid cola.
What is Mr Hall's intention: to inform, to warn or to persuade?
Find two reasons Mr Hall gives.
Rewrite as advice: Don't use your phone at night. -> You should...
practice_answers: Sleep helps memory; screens at night keep you awake.
You should switch off your phone at night.
3E-05.mission: Listen to a classmate's one-minute advice talk (exams, sport, screens). Take notes in a grid: intention, three arguments, one example. Report back to the group.
can_do: I can identify the speaker's intention.
I can note the main arguments.
I can take short notes with key words and symbols.
3E-05.memory: Write five note-taking symbols and what they mean.

3E-06.hook: TWO TEENS, TWO OPINIONS: WHO DO YOU AGREE WITH?
vocab: I understand your point of view.
Unlike Mia, Léo has no uniform.
Mia likes it whereas Léo doesn't.
However, he agrees on one point.
On the one hand, it saves time.
On the other hand, it's expensive.
Don't judge people by their clothes.

grammar.title: Agreeing, disagreeing and comparing
grammar.rule: Agree: I agree with... / That's true. Disagree: I disagree with... / I don't think so. Partly: I partly agree, but... Compare: both..., unlike..., whereas..., on the one hand... on the other hand...
examples: I agree with Mia: it saves time.
Unlike Mia, Léo prefers his own clothes.
Mia likes uniforms whereas Léo doesn't.

3E-06.pronunciation: To disagree politely, use a soft voice and a falling tone: I'm not sure I agree...
3E-06.did_you_know: Most secondary schools in the UK have a uniform, often with a blazer and a tie in the school's colours.
3E-06.model:
Mia (UK): I think school uniforms are great. Everybody looks the same, so nobody judges your clothes. Moreover, it saves time in the morning.
Léo (France): I disagree with Mia. In France we don't wear uniforms and I like it: my clothes show my personality. However, I agree that some students judge others' clothes.

listening.title: Important people
questions: How has speaker B's relationship with his brother changed?
Why do speaker C and her friend help each other?
How does speaker D keep in touch with his friend now?
answers: They ignored each other at school; now they get on well
She is good at languages and her friend is good at maths
listening.fallback:
Speaker B: My brother is four years older. At school we ignored each other, but now we get on well and we watch football together.
Speaker C: My best friend and I met when we were five. I'm good at languages and she's good at maths, so we help each other with homework.
Speaker D: A boy moved into my street when I was ten. His family left a couple of years ago, so now we keep in touch on Facebook.

go_further.title: Foreign exchange emails
go_further.task: Read Simon's and Fran's emails. Find one positive and one negative point about Fran's host family.

practice: Find one argument for uniforms.
Find one argument against uniforms.
Find one point Mia and Léo both accept.
Complete: ___ Mia, Léo doesn't wear a uniform.
practice_answers: Nobody judges your clothes / it saves time.
3E-06.mission: Read two short documents with different points of view (uniforms, phones at school...). Fill a two-column chart, then write three sentences: both..., unlike..., I agree with... because...
can_do: I can find the arguments in two short texts.
I can compare two points of view.
I can say if I agree and why.
3E-06.memory: Write three ways to agree and three ways to disagree politely.

3E-07.hook: GREAT IDEA... OR NOT? WEIGH THE PROS AND CONS!
vocab: The main advantage is the price.
The only drawback is the noise.
What are the limits of this idea?
It's expensive but it's worth it.

grammar.title: should, could, might
grammar.rule: should = advice: We should try it. could = possibility or suggestion: It could help students. might = weaker possibility: It might be too expensive. Always + verb without to.
examples: We should organise a bike bus.
It could reduce pollution.
Some parents might not agree.

3E-07.pronunciation: should, could, would: the l is silent! Say /shud/, /kud/, /wud/.
3E-07.did_you_know: Every year, on 22 September, many towns around the world celebrate World Car-Free Day.
3E-07.model:
Ava: Our school wants a car-free day once a month. What do you think?
Ryan: It could reduce pollution and we might walk more.
Ava: True, but it might be difficult for students who live far away.
Ryan: We should organise a bike bus with teachers.
Ava: Good idea. The benefits are bigger than the drawbacks.

listening.title: Sports centres
questions: How long has Grange Park Sports Centre been open?
How many classes a week are included in the membership at Maya's centre?
What is the main drawback of Bill's centre?
answers: It is more expensive than other gyms in the area
listening.fallback:
Maya: Grange Park is a small centre, open for ten years, with lots of classes: yoga, Zumba, dance and now flamenco. There's a sauna and a café. Membership includes the gym and two classes a week, but bring your own towel.
Bill: Our gym is very big, with new machines, a swimming pool and four specialists for exercise and diet. It's more expensive than other gyms in the area, but our services are better.

go_further.title: Theme parks
go_further.task: Listen to Andy Wells. Note one advantage of his job and one difficulty.

practice: Complete with should, could or might: We ___ ask the town for help. (advice)
Complete: It ___ rain that day. (weak possibility)
Give one advantage and one drawback of a car-free day.
Write a sentence with "on the other hand".
practice_answers: Réponse possible : less pollution / difficult for students who live far away.
3E-07.mission: In groups of four, discuss an initiative (car-free day, no phones at lunch, school garden): two students defend the advantages, two explain the limits. Agree on a recommendation with should.
can_do: I can give advantages and limits of an idea.
I can use should, could and might.
I can reach a decision with my group.
3E-07.memory: Write two advantages and two limits of one initiative with should, could or might.

3E-08.hook: IT HAPPENED... AND IT CHANGED EVERYTHING.
vocab: While I was texting, he took my phone.
As a result, I was late.
I missed the bus, so I walked.
Since then, I've been more careful.
I realised my bag was open.
He has to retake the exam.

grammar.title: Past simple and past continuous
grammar.rule: Past continuous (was / were + -ing) = background action: I was texting a friend. Past simple = short event: someone stole my phone. While + past continuous, when + past simple. Consequences: so, as a result, since then.
examples: I was walking to school when I saw the accident.
While we were waiting, it started to rain.
As a result, I was late.

3E-08.pronunciation: was is weak in the middle of a sentence: I /wuz/ walking. Stress the verb: I was WALKING when I SAW him.
3E-08.did_you_know: In the UK, the emergency number is 999, but 112 also works, as in France.
3E-08.model: Last year, I was walking to school when I saw an old man fall. Suddenly, everybody stopped, but nobody moved. I called for help and I stayed with him. As a result, the ambulance arrived quickly. Since then, I have done a first-aid course, and I feel ready to help.

listening.title: Difficult situations
questions: What will probably happen if Ryan failed his Economics exam?
Why did Bonzo run into the road?
What might help to find the phone thief?
answers: He will have to retake the whole course
He ran after a ball that went over the hedge
The CCTV camera at the school entrance
listening.fallback:
Mother: Ryan, you failed your Economics exam? You were out until four in the morning!
Ryan: I know. Now I'll probably have to retake the whole course. I'll talk to my teacher.
Megan: This morning Bonzo chased a ball over the hedge into the road and a car hit him. The vet couldn't save him.
Boy: Dad, someone stole your phone outside school while I was texting. There's a CCTV camera at the entrance, so maybe it filmed him.

practice: Complete: I ___ (text) a friend when the thief ___ (take) my phone.
Join with so: I missed the bus. I was late.
Write a consequence: Bonzo ran into the road. As a result...
Ask the question: What / you / do / when it happened?
practice_answers: I missed the bus, so I was late.
Réponse possible : As a result, a car hit him.
What did you do when it happened?
starters: It was... and I was...ing when...
3E-08.mission: Tell your group about an experience (real or imagined: a trip, a problem, a surprise) in one to two minutes: the background, the event, the consequences and what you learnt. Listeners ask one question.
can_do: I can tell a story with past simple and past continuous.
I can explain the consequences of an event.
I can say what I learnt from an experience.
3E-08.memory: Write a three-sentence story with while, suddenly and as a result.

3E-09.hook: ONE DOCUMENT, ONE MINUTE: THE WHOLE GROUP KNOWS!
vocab: The carnival takes place in August.
Our neighbours cook for the party.
In short, it's a festival of light.

grammar.title: Synthesising for a group
grammar.rule: Introduce: This document is about... Main ideas: According to the text... / The first point is... Link: also, whereas, both. Conclude: In short / To sum up... Keep only who, what, where, when and why.
examples: This text is about Diwali, the festival of lights.
According to the speaker, the carnival is in August.
In short, both festivals bring people together.

3E-09.pronunciation: Pause between your main ideas and let your voice go down at the end of each one: listeners know an idea is finished.
3E-09.did_you_know: The Notting Hill Carnival started in the 1960s. It celebrates Caribbean culture and is one of the biggest street festivals in Europe.
3E-09.model: This text is about Diwali, the festival of lights. According to the text, Hindus, Sikhs and Jains celebrate it in October or November. People light lamps, share sweets and watch fireworks. In Leicester, in the UK, thousands of people come to see the lights. In short, Diwali is a festival of light, family and sharing.

listening.title: Celebrations
questions: When does the Notting Hill Carnival take place?
What anniversary does speaker C's family celebrate?
Where do the neighbours at speaker E's street party come from?
answers: From India, China and several African countries
listening.fallback:
Speaker B: Every August there's the Notting Hill Carnival in London, with costumes, steel bands and dancing. But watch out for pickpockets!
Speaker C: For my grandparents' golden wedding anniversary, we're hiring a boat for a river trip, with a picnic and music from the 1960s.
Speaker E: For the Royal Wedding in June, we're having a street party. Our neighbours from India, China and Africa are bringing food.

practice: Find the who, what, where and when of the Diwali text.
Shorten to keep the key idea: In Leicester, in the UK, thousands and thousands of people come every year to see the beautiful lights.
Complete: ___ the text, people share sweets.
Write a one-sentence summary of Diwali with In short.
practice_answers: Hindus, Sikhs and Jains / festival of lights / India and Leicester / October or November
Thousands of people see the lights in Leicester every year.
Réponse possible : In short, Diwali is a festival of light and sharing.
3E-09.mission: In groups of four, each student reads a different short document about a celebration (Carnival, Diwali, Thanksgiving, Burns Night), takes notes and gives a 45-second synthesis. The group finds two things in common.
can_do: I can find the main ideas in a short document.
I can sum them up in my own words.
I can present a clear synthesis to my group.
3E-09.memory: Write the five synthesis questions (who, what, where, when, why) and three linking expressions.

3E-10.hook: SLOW DOWN, PAUSE, AND EVERYONE GETS IT!
vocab: Make a pause after each idea.
Speak loud enough for the class.

grammar.title: Chunks and pauses
grammar.rule: Split long sentences into chunks of 3 to 6 words. Pause (/) between chunks, stress one key word in each chunk and slow down for numbers.
examples: Only one TENTH / of the cells in your BODY / are HUMAN.
Most of them / are really HELPFUL.
About SEVEN octillion / CELLS!

3E-10.pronunciation: Numbers need time: say about SEVEN octillion and a THIRD of a millimetre slowly, and stress the number.
3E-10.did_you_know: Many good speakers talk at about 120 to 150 words per minute. When we are nervous, we often speak much faster.
3E-10.model: Did you know / that your body / is home to millions of bacteria? / Don't panic! / Most of them / are really helpful. / They help you / digest your food. / Amazing, isn't it?

listening.title: Amazing facts
questions: What proportion of the cells in your body are human?
Roughly how many cells does a human body have?
How long are the mites that live in eyelashes?
answers: About seven octillion (7 followed by 27 zeros)
About a third of a millimetre
listening.fallback:
A: Listen to this! Only about one tenth of the cells in your body are human. Most of the others are bacteria.
B: Bacteria? That's horrible!
A: Don't worry, most of them help us digest food. And a body has about seven octillion cells.
A: Also, tiny mites live in our eyelashes. They're about a third of a millimetre long.
B: Stop! That's disgusting!

practice: Mark the pauses (/): Most bacteria in your body are helpful because they help you digest food.
Underline the key word in each chunk of the model text.
Read slowly: 7 octillion - one tenth - a third of a millimetre.
Time yourself: read the model text in about 20 seconds.
practice_answers: Most bacteria in your body / are helpful / because they help you / digest food.
Réponse possible : KNOW, BODY, BACTERIA, PANIC, HELPFUL, DIGEST, AMAZING
3E-10.mission: Prepare a 45-second Amazing Fact presentation. Mark chunks and key words, rehearse twice, then present. The group gives feedback on pace, pauses and stress.
can_do: I can speak at a pace my audience can follow.
I can pause between groups of words.
I can stress key words and numbers.
3E-10.memory: Write three tips for speaking clearly and practise them with one sentence.
